mcq.q: The class mark (mid-value) of the class 10–19 is:
mcq.explain: Class mark = (lower limit + upper limit)/2 = (10 + 19)/2 = 14.5. It represents every observation of the class in calculations such as the mean. The width of the class (9) is a different quantity.
mcq.fast: Class mark = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2.

mcq.q: The class mark (mid-value) of the class 110–130 is:
mcq.explain: Class mark = (lower limit + upper limit)/2 = (110 + 130)/2 = 120. It represents every observation of the class in calculations such as the mean. The width of the class (20) is a different quantity.
mcq.fast: Class mark = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2.

mcq.q: For the inclusive classes 20–44, 45–69, 70–94, 95–119, …, the lower class boundary of the class 95–119 is:
mcq.explain: In inclusive classes there is a gap of 1 between one upper limit and the next lower limit. Half the gap (0.5) is subtracted from every lower limit and added to every upper limit. So the lower boundary of 95–119 is 94.5. Boundaries make the classes continuous (exclusive).
mcq.fast: Lower boundary = lower limit − 0.5; upper boundary = upper limit + 0.5 (gap of 1).

mcq.q: For the inclusive classes 0–24, 25–49, 50–74, 75–99, …, the upper class boundary of the class 50–74 is:
mcq.explain: In inclusive classes there is a gap of 1 between one upper limit and the next lower limit. Half the gap (0.5) is subtracted from every lower limit and added to every upper limit. So the upper boundary of 50–74 is 74.5. Boundaries make the classes continuous (exclusive).
mcq.fast: Lower boundary = lower limit − 0.5; upper boundary = upper limit + 0.5 (gap of 1).

mcq.q: A class 40–50 has frequency 11. Its frequency density is:
mcq.explain: Frequency density = class frequency ÷ class width = 11 ÷ 10 = 1.1. It is used to draw histograms correctly when classes have unequal widths, because the area (not the height) of each bar must show the frequency.
mcq.fast: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.

mcq.q: A class 10–20 has frequency 19. Its frequency density is:
mcq.explain: Frequency density = class frequency ÷ class width = 19 ÷ 10 = 1.9. It is used to draw histograms correctly when classes have unequal widths, because the area (not the height) of each bar must show the frequency.
mcq.fast: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.

mcq.q: Frequency distribution — 0–20: 24; 20–40: 30; 40–60: 13; 60–80: 27; 80–100: 30; 100–120: 19. The relative frequency of the class 20–40, as a percentage, is about:
mcq.explain: Total frequency N = 143. Relative frequency = class frequency ÷ N = 30 ÷ 143 = 0.2098, i.e. about 20.98%. Using the cumulative frequency (54) instead of the class frequency is a common slip.
mcq.fast: Add the frequencies once (N = 143), then f ÷ N × 100.

mcq.q: Frequency distribution — 0–20: 11; 20–40: 14; 40–60: 14; 60–80: 10; 80–100: 16; 100–120: 9. The relative frequency of the class 40–60, as a percentage, is about:
mcq.explain: Total frequency N = 74. Relative frequency = class frequency ÷ N = 14 ÷ 74 = 0.1892, i.e. about 18.92%. Using the cumulative frequency (39) instead of the class frequency is a common slip.
mcq.fast: Add the frequencies once (N = 74), then f ÷ N × 100.

mcq.q: Frequency distribution — 10–35: 20; 35–60: 18; 60–85: 3; 85–110: 14; 110–135: 7; 135–160: 3; 160–185: 20. The number of observations less than 135 is:
mcq.explain: This is a less-than cumulative frequency. Add the frequencies of all classes up to the one ending at 135: 20 + 18 + 3 + 14 + 7 = 62. Cumulative frequencies are exactly what an ogive plots against the class boundaries, so read the class limits carefully before adding.
mcq.fast: Keep a running total from the correct end of the table.

mcq.explain: This is a less-than cumulative frequency. Add the frequencies of all classes up to the one ending at 40: 7 + 2 + 6 + 8 = 23. Cumulative frequencies are exactly what an ogive plots against the class boundaries, so read the class limits carefully before adding.
mcq.fast: Keep a running total from the correct end of the table.

mcq.q: Frequency distribution — 100–120: 9; 120–140: 21; 140–160: 23; 160–180: 4; 180–200: 25; 200–220: 24. The number of observations less than 140 is:
mcq.explain: This is a less-than cumulative frequency. Add the frequencies of all classes up to the one ending at 140: 9 + 21 = 30. Cumulative frequencies are exactly what an ogive plots against the class boundaries, so read the class limits carefully before adding.

mcq.q: Monthly spending (₹): Wheat 1,200, Rice 500, Pulses 1,000, Oilseeds 600, Others 700. In a pie chart, the angle for Wheat is:
mcq.explain: Total = ₹4,000. Each item gets a share of 360° in proportion to its value: Wheat angle = 1,200/4,000 × 360° = 108°. Writing the percentage (30%) as degrees is the classic mistake. All the angles together must add up to 360°.
mcq.fast: Angle = (value ÷ total) × 360; or percentage × 3.6.

mcq.q: Monthly spending (₹): Food 2,700, Rent 1,200, Education 600, Transport 200, Savings 700. In a pie chart, the angle for Rent is:
mcq.explain: Total = ₹5,400. Each item gets a share of 360° in proportion to its value: Rent angle = 1,200/5,400 × 360° = 80°. Writing the percentage (22.22%) as degrees is the classic mistake. All the angles together must add up to 360°.
mcq.fast: Angle = (value ÷ total) × 360; or percentage × 3.6.

mcq.q: The class marks of a distribution are 76, 84, 92, 100. The lower limit of the class whose mark is 76 is (exclusive classes):
mcq.explain: Consecutive class marks differ by the class width: 84 − 76 = 8. A class extends half the width on each side of its mark, so the lower limit is 76 − 4 = 72. Adding or subtracting the full width overshoots into the next class.
mcq.fast: Width = difference of marks; limit = mark ± width/2.

mcq.q: The class marks of a distribution are 14, 18, 22, 26. The lower limit of the class whose mark is 26 is (exclusive classes):
mcq.explain: Consecutive class marks differ by the class width: 18 − 14 = 4. A class extends half the width on each side of its mark, so the lower limit is 26 − 2 = 24. Adding or subtracting the full width overshoots into the next class.
mcq.fast: Width = difference of marks; limit = mark ± width/2.

mcq.q: The smallest observation is 36 and the largest is 408. Using exclusive classes of width 15 starting at 36, how many classes are needed so that every observation is included?
mcq.explain: Range = 408 − 36 = 372. Classes 36–51, 51–66, … each include the lower limit and exclude the upper limit. 372 ÷ 15 = 24.8; rounding up gives 25 classes. Too few classes would leave the largest values outside the table.
mcq.fast: Classes = range ÷ width, rounded up; add one if the maximum falls exactly on an upper limit.

mcq.q: The smallest observation is 88 and the largest is 285. Using exclusive classes of width 25 starting at 88, how many classes are needed so that every observation is included?
mcq.explain: Range = 285 − 88 = 197. Classes 88–113, 113–138, … each include the lower limit and exclude the upper limit. 197 ÷ 25 = 7.88; rounding up gives 8 classes. Too few classes would leave the largest values outside the table.
mcq.fast: Classes = range ÷ width, rounded up; add one if the maximum falls exactly on an upper limit.

mcq.q: A percentage bar diagram is drawn for: Raw material 280, Wages 250, Power 550, Overheads 90. The length of the Overheads segment, as a percentage of the bar, is about:
mcq.explain: In a percentage (sub-divided) bar each component is shown as its share of the total. Total = 1,170; Overheads = 90/1,170 × 100 = 7.69%. The whole bar always represents 100%, and the segments are stacked in the same order in every bar.
mcq.fast: Segment share = value ÷ total × 100.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a limitation of statistics?
options: It does not study individual cases
It deals with aggregates of facts
mcq.explain: Statistics deals with groups (aggregates); a single isolated figure about one individual is not a statistic, which is why it does not study individuals. So the correct answer is "It does not study individual cases". The other options describe different terms, so read the key word in the question carefully before choosing.
